w: What's tested Why denture "bite" is different: the goal is to keep a loose plate in the mouth, so balance means it doesn't tip Support, stability and retention, and why stability (no sliding sideways) matters most What holds a denture in: the thin film of saliva and the seal at the edges, a good fit, and most of all the patient's muscle control How the bone shrinks after teeth are lost (upper jaw up and in, lower jaw down and out), and why dentures are often set in crossbite The setups: balanced, non-balanced (also called neutrocentric) and lingualized, who gets which, and the table comparing them Why a denture's bite is built and checked on an articulator, not in the mouth (Hanau's Realeff), and which of Thielemann's factors you can't change Kinds of denture teeth, their cusp angles (30-33°, 12-22°, 0°) and how they're picked This lecture (11/5) is about bites on dentures. The class hasn't had its denture course yet (it starts in January), so Dr. Givan explained what dentures are first. The big idea: for a denture, the bite's job is to keep the denture in the mouth and let the patient function. A full denture just sits on the gums, with nothing holding it. Patients who call them "plates" aren't far off: imagine a dinner plate trying to stay put in someone's mouth. Denture words Denture teeth aren't real teeth, just tooth-colored plastic. They sit in the pink denture base, which fits over the gums; the better it fits, the better it stays in. The edges that run up into the cheek and lip pocket are the flange, and the edge of the flange, where moving tissue meets tissue that doesn't move, is the peripheral border. Someone with no teeth is edentulous; they wear complete (or full) dentures. If some teeth are left, it's a partial denture. When teeth are lost, the jawbone shrinks (resorption). Losing a lot makes eating very hard, especially with the lower denture. That problem is what led to dental implants about 50 years ago: to hold dentures in. A short history What did occlusion have to do with early dentures? "Practically none." (The history slides say "No test questions": know the point, not the dates.) The first ones were carved from wood or ivory, mostly for looks. Later ones had hinges or springs at the back, including Fauchard's (the father of dentistry), but you couldn't really eat or talk with them. George Washington's dentures weren't wooden: his dentist, John Greenwood, carved them from bone and ivory with gold bases and springs, and the Washingtons' letters (at UAB's Reynolds Historical Library) complain about the same soreness patients have today. Later, dentures fit well enough to hold by suction (Gardette noticed that air pressure held a well-fitting base in). Porcelain came next: Duchâteau's porcelain dentures (about 1774) chipped and looked too white, and in 1808 Fonzi made single porcelain teeth that lasted in the mouth. Bonwill made the first real try at a denture bite: keep the teeth touching all the time so the denture stays in. That's why he's the "father of articulation." Old ideas about tooth shape stuck around: matching the patient's personality (molds are still called "bold" or "soft") and matching the face shape (square, tapered, ovoid). In the early 1900s Gysi, working with the company that became Dentsply, perfected balanced dentures; his Trubyte teeth are still sold. The point: a denture's bite is about not tipping, not about guiding forces the way it is with real teeth. Why the denture bite is different Without teeth, there's no feedback from the teeth and their ligaments, so patients only vaguely sense where they are. Think of a denture wearer as having one upper tooth and one lower tooth: each denture moves as one piece. So the teeth are arranged to keep the denture from tipping when they touch. That's what balance means: touching on both sides at once, so a chewing movement to the right doesn't flip the denture up on the left. Those balancing contacts are exactly what we avoid on natural teeth. What holds a denture in Suction and saliva help a well-fitting denture stick. The slides say what helps most: the thin film of saliva between the denture and the gums, and the pull of that film at the edges; suction, vacuum and stickiness help less. A good seal around the edges keeps air from leaking under it. All of it depends on the patient's saliva (it changes with age) and on a good fit, and chewing or a hot drink undoes most of it. The real key is the patient's muscle control: some people keep even bad dentures in and eat fine; others can't manage the best one. "Muscle control is likely to be the most important factor." Most of the day the teeth are apart, so those forces are what hold the denture then. Bony bulges (undercuts) help only a little and can make it sore, and a loose denture speeds up bone loss. What makes it harder What stops it tipping. Tall, wide ridges, a deep palate (a big help for the upper denture) and the right kind of seal at the back give the denture something to hold onto; so do an inner surface that fits the gums closely and teeth that touch without pushing the denture around. As bone is lost, it gets harder. A post dam (posterior palatal seal) at the back of an upper denture presses into the soft tissue to make up for the plastic shrinking; milled dentures often don't need one. "All removable is movable." Dentures always move a little. The gums are soft and squish when the teeth bite, so the denture shifts. Hanau called this the Realeff ("resiliency and like effect"). That's why a denture's bite is built on an articulator, not in the mouth. How the bone shrinks. The upper jaw shrinks up and in, so it gets smaller. The lower jaw shrinks down and out, so at tooth level it ends up bigger. Front upper: up and back (in). Back upper: up and toward the middle. Front lower: down and forward. Back lower: down and away from the middle (out). Because denture teeth go over the ridge, they're often set in crossbite, and that's fine. Jaw sizes. Class I: the jaws match. Class II: the lower jaw is small and set back. Class III: the lower jaw is bigger and forward. When bone loss makes the lower jaw look bigger than the upper, it's a pseudo-Class III. Also: the tongue gets bigger after teeth are lost, which mostly troubles the lower denture. And people whose teeth were just pulled aren't easier: there may not be enough room between the jaws for the denture. Support, stability and retention The three things to remember about any removable denture: Support resists pushing down into the gums. The palate on top, and the cheek-side shelf and the pad behind the last tooth on the bottom, handle it well; the ridges themselves don't. Retention resists being pulled off, like peanut butter pulling the denture loose, or the tongue lifting the lower one. Patients notice it most, but it doesn't hurt. Stability resists sliding sideways. It's the most important: a denture that shifts when you bite really hurts, and patients can't eat. Implants are great at stability; even two can change a patient's life. We chew side to side, not straight up and down like a shark, which makes stability harder. The denture's bite helps most with stability. For support, the teeth should touch on both sides, evenly and at the same time, pushing the denture onto the ridges: flat teeth do it with a flat plane, cusped teeth by fitting cusp into groove. Centric relation and centric occlusion When a denture wearer bites, the muscles seat the jaw joints, so centric relation is easy to find. The teeth fitting together with the joints seated is called centric occlusion. We don't say MIP for dentures, because MIP is a position the nerves and muscles learn from real teeth. When the dentures close, usually only the back teeth touch; the front bone (premaxilla) doesn't handle force well, so the front teeth are mainly for looks. The three setups Balanced (also called bilateral balance or "anatomic" occlusion): the teeth touch when you close and in every sliding movement, on both sides at once. Definition: both sides, front and back teeth, touching at the same time in centric and eccentric positions. With tall-cusped teeth the front teeth can even touch when you slide forward. It needs a semi-adjustable articulator set up to match the patient (a facebow and a protrusive record), and skill. Non-balanced (the slides also call it neutrocentric: flatten everything and keep the forces in the middle): the teeth touch only when you close; in any sliding movement they separate. Use flat (0°) teeth on a flat plane parallel to the ridges, no curve, no front-tooth contact, and set the articulator's condyle angle to zero, so the patient's own joint angle pulls the teeth apart as they move. Set the teeth as far toward the tongue as it allows, make them 40% narrower to ease the load on the ridge, keep them parallel to the denture bases (and tell the patient not to bite with the front teeth), use cuspless teeth, and maybe skip the lower second molars where the jaw starts curving up. Easy to set up. Why does non-balanced work? While chewing, food sits between the teeth, so there's no balance anyway. Denture patients learn to chew on both sides, chew straight up and down, take small bites and chew with the premolars, not the front teeth. An old saying sums it up: "Enter bolus, exit balance." Lingualized: the middle ground, and the one you'll probably use most. The upper teeth (semi-anatomic) have a long tongue-side cusp that works like a mortar and pestle against flat or wide-grooved lower teeth (0-12°), and the cheek-side cusps don't touch. It's easy to set and can be balanced (touching when you close and when you slide) or non-balanced (touching only when you close). Can the front teeth touch? In class he said never; the slides say not really, though it can be made up for. Pick non-balanced for a lot of bone loss, flabby gums, poor coordination or difficult jaw sizes; balanced for good ridges, firm gums and good coordination. Upsides, from the slides: the contacts move half a tooth toward the tongue, so the force lands over the ridge; one contact point; less rubbing; room for food to escape; simpler side-to-side contacts; and it works with any ridge, so for almost anyone. Downside: with fewer contacts it can wear faster and the bite can collapse a little. The four setups compared. The slides rate them from − to +++. Balanced is best for looks (+++) and stability while chewing (++), but scores − on simple technique, easy records, low sideways force, easy adjusting, Class II and III jaws, and centered force. Balanced lingualized: + for looks, biting through food, stability while chewing and easy adjusting. Non-balanced lingualized: + for nearly everything, ++ for easy adjusting, − only for stability while chewing. Non-balanced: − for looks, biting through food and stability while chewing, but ++ for simple technique, easy records and low sideways force, +++ for easy adjusting, and + for Class II and III jaws and centered force. Building balance Rudolph Hanau, an engineer, made balance easier. He saw that the soft gums keep moving (the Realeff), so you can't build or mark a denture's bite in the mouth: with articulating paper, the denture tips and everything marks. It's done on an articulator, and fine-tuned by putting the dentures back on the articulator (a clinical remount), never by grinding in the mouth. His balanced dentures also had heavy contacts on the first molars to make up for the squishy gums and joints. He tied the five factors together (Hanau's quint), and Thielemann's formula (spelled Thielmann in the Review lecture) shows the math: steepen the plane, for example, and you flatten the curve or the cusps to keep the teeth touching. For dentures we use them to keep teeth together; for natural teeth, to keep them apart. Two factors are fixed: the jaw joint's angle, and the plane of the teeth, lined up with the eyes and with Camper's line from the nose to the ear (it changes only a little). Three can vary: the front-teeth guidance (rarely used, since the front teeth usually don't touch), the curve and the cusp angle. So balance comes from the curve, the cusp angle and a little plane. To set up balance, the joint angle comes from a forward-bite record. Denture teeth Porcelain: the best looking and barely wears, so it keeps the bite height, but it can chip, it's hard to set and adjust, it clicks, and it doesn't bond to the base, so it's held with pins (front teeth) or holes with undercuts (back teeth). Composite and cross-linked plastic: the most common, what most good dentures use; layered for a natural look, doesn't chip, quieter, easy to adjust and polish, bonds to the base, costs more. It still wears: in 5-7 years the back teeth wear into a reverse curve and chew poorly. Acrylic: cheap, bonds, easy to shape and can be ground down to fit a tight space, but wears and stains; mostly for temporary dentures. Worn denture teeth let the bite close down, so wear resistance matters. Picking the teeth Teeth come in matched sets from a mold chart. You pick the upper front mold, and the chart tells you the lower front mold and the back teeth for each setup. So "the denture occlusion is entirely based upon" that upper front mold, and it's picked mostly for looks: "soft" or "bold," square, tapering or ovoid. Helpful guides: the wax rim tried in the mouth shows lip support, where the front edges go, the midline, where the canines go, and the plane the teeth are set to. Old rules of thumb, like the front tooth being about 1/16 of the cheekbone-to-cheekbone width (Berry, 1906) or measuring across the nose, aren't scientific, but they tend to look good. The back teeth depend on the setup and on the patient's muscle control, ridges, jaw sizes, the room between the jaws, and whether they've worn dentures before (everyone starts over with new ones). Pick a natural shade, not "headlights." Denture teeth are usually a bit smaller than real ones. For the back teeth the slides check six things: a color that matches the front teeth, narrower than natural teeth, a height that fits the room between the jaws and matches the canine, a length that runs from behind the canine to the pad at the back of the ridge, the cusp angle, and the material. Tooth shapes. Anatomic teeth have tall cusps (30-33°), look the most natural, allow balance, resist the denture rotating and spread the load, but need more records, setup and skill, push the denture sideways more, are hard to fine-tune, and their results don't last as the denture settles and cheap ones wear. Semi-anatomic teeth (also called functional or anatoline) have lower cusps (about 12-22°); the front teeth can't touch unless the plane or curve makes up for it. Flat teeth (0°, also called cuspless, zero-degree, rational, flat-plane or monoline) push the denture sideways the least, suit any jaw size and crossbites, are easy to adjust and suit patients with poor muscle control; but they cut food poorly (more pressure on the ridges), are hard to balance and some patients don't like them. What the evidence says Tall-cusped teeth look best and chew a little better, but flat, non-balanced dentures work just as well for patients, who stay well fed. Chewing is just one factor in choosing. Most patients want to smile at their grandkids and enjoy a meal. A 2013 review the slides cite (Abduo) found patients prefer cusped teeth set balanced or lingualized over flat non-balanced ones, though the research isn't conclusive and every setup generally works. Partial dentures The more teeth lost, the more you think like a full denture (keep it stable). The more teeth left, the more you think like natural teeth (canine guidance or group function, back teeth separating), because the teeth are in charge. Implants add more to think about, and every removable denture moves a little. The big picture: a denture's bite is about keeping it in the mouth. Each denture works as one piece, balance means it doesn't tip, and stability matters most.
